betaLB: Example Using the Effect Size Functions

Ivan Jacob Agaloos Pesigan

Source: vignettes/example-es-lb.Rmd
example-es-lb.Rmd

In this example, a multiple regression model is fitted using program quality ratings (QUALITY) as the regressand/outcome variable and number of published articles attributed to the program faculty members (NARTIC), percent of faculty members holding research grants (PCTGRT), and percentage of program graduates who received support (PCTSUPP) as regressor/predictor variables using a data set from 1982 ratings of 46 doctoral programs in psychology in the USA (National Research Council, 1982).

library(package = betaLB)
df <- betaLB::nas1982

Fit the regression model using the lm() function. 

object <- stats::lm(formula = QUALITY ~ NARTIC + PCTGRT + PCTSUPP, data = df)

Estimate the standardized regression slopes.

The effect size functions take the output of BetaLB() and use its type and control.

std <- BetaLB(object = object, type = "robust", alpha = 0.05)

Semipartial correlations 

summary(object = SCorLB(object = std, alpha = 0.05))
#> Call:
#> SCorLB(object = std, alpha = 0.05)
#> 
#> Semipartial correlations with ROBUST likelihood intervals:
#>            est   2.5%  97.5%
#> NARTIC  0.4312 0.3070 0.5680
#> PCTGRT  0.3430 0.2163 0.4860
#> PCTSUPP 0.2385 0.1077 0.3859

Squared semipartial correlations

The SCorSqLB() function squares the signed-semipartial interval as a set. If the signed interval contains zero, the lower limit of the squared interval is zero.

SCorSqLB(object = std, level = 0.95)
#>               est      lower     upper
#> NARTIC  0.1858925 0.09422306 0.3226656
#> PCTGRT  0.1176542 0.04678291 0.2361584
#> PCTSUPP 0.0568722 0.01160043 0.1489431

Squared partial correlations 

summary(object = PCorLB(object = std, alpha = 0.05))
#> Call:
#> PCorLB(object = std, alpha = 0.05)
#> 
#> Squared partial correlations with ROBUST likelihood intervals:
#>            est   2.5%  97.5%
#> NARTIC  0.4874 0.2937 0.6525
#> PCTGRT  0.3757 0.1801 0.5634
#> PCTSUPP 0.2254 0.0426 0.4578

Improvement in R-squared

The improvement in R-squared of regressor j is sr^{2}_{j}. The blocks argument gives the improvement of a set of regressors.

summary(
  object = DeltaRSqLB(
    object = std,
    alpha = 0.05,
    blocks = list(grants = c("PCTGRT", "PCTSUPP"))
  )
)
#> Call:
#> DeltaRSqLB(object = std, alpha = 0.05, blocks = list(grants = c("PCTGRT", 
#>     "PCTSUPP")))
#> 
#> Improvement in R-squared with ROBUST likelihood intervals:
#>                 est   2.5%  97.5%
#> NARTIC       0.1859 0.0942 0.3227
#> PCTGRT       0.1177 0.0468 0.2362
#> PCTSUPP      0.0569 0.0116 0.1489
#> block:grants 0.2236 0.0839 0.4585

Cohen’s f-squared and local f-squared 

summary(object = FSqLB(object = std, alpha = 0.05))
#> Call:
#> FSqLB(object = std, alpha = 0.05)
#> 
#> Cohen's f-squared (fsq) and local f-squared with ROBUST likelihood intervals:
#>            est   2.5%   97.5%
#> fsq     4.1158 1.3593 11.1105
#> NARTIC  0.9510 0.4158  1.8774
#> PCTGRT  0.6019 0.2197  1.2903
#> PCTSUPP 0.2909 0.0445  0.8444

Extracting estimates and confidence intervals 

scor <- SCorLB(object = std, alpha = 0.05)
stats::coef(object = scor)
#>    NARTIC    PCTGRT   PCTSUPP 
#> 0.4311525 0.3430075 0.2384789
stats::confint(object = scor, level = 0.95)
#>             2.5 %    97.5 %
#> NARTIC  0.3069578 0.5680366
#> PCTGRT  0.2162936 0.4859613
#> PCTSUPP 0.1077053 0.3859315

References

Dudgeon, P. (2017). Some improvements in confidence intervals for standardized regression coefficients. Psychometrika, 82(4), 928–951. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-017-9563-z
National Research Council. (1982). An assessment of research-doctorate programs in the United States: Social and behavioral sciences. National Academies Press. https://doi.org/10.17226/9781
